content:
<belle_riviere_setting>
The setting is Belle Rivière, Louisiana in the 1980s. The town is draped in Spanish moss, thick summer heat, neon bleeding over wet streets, and the particular kind of silence that comes from a population that has collectively agreed not to ask too many questions.

Belle Rivière is not a safe town. It is, however, very pretty. People go missing here. Certain families have been here too long and look too young. Certain streets feel wrong after dark. Certain rich locals are impossible to look at for too long without feeling like you missed something important.

Humans live here too. Most of them do not know what is actually sharing the town with them. The ones who get too close tend to stay quiet — either because nobody would believe them, or because they have lived in Belle Rivière long enough to understand that knowing is more dangerous than not knowing.

The 1980s in Louisiana meant the oil boom had collapsed. Old money got precarious. New money disappeared overnight. The families who had been here for centuries watched and waited, as they always have.
</belle_riviere_setting>

content:
<territorial_rules>
Belle Rivière operates on strictly enforced territorial boundaries. Each faction claims its slice and does not venture into another's without reason.

The older families occupy grand plantation estates, old manors, restored theaters, private clubs. Their holdings connect through underground passages. Other factions have their own tunnel systems — less grand, more lived-in, dug into the land like they intend to stay forever.

The human parts of town operate as a loose neutral buffer zone. Fights do not happen in front of humans. This is less a law and more an agreement forged out of mutual self-interest: a loud brawl draws police attention, and police attention is inconvenient for everyone.

A proper neutral zone does not yet exist. That is a 2000s problem.
</territorial_rules>

Most of the strange locals pass as ordinary well enough for daily life. They are treated as wealthy eccentrics, old families with odd hours, or simply people with too much money and too much privacy.

People go missing. This is treated as a local tragedy and a statistical inevitability. Someone is always trying to keep the numbers down. It does not always work.

content:
<aesthetic_1980s>
Belle Rivière in the 1980s looks like a Southern Gothic postcard and sounds like a synth-heavy nightmare. Old money and new noise. Ancient bloodlines and local-access television.

Spanish moss over wrought iron fences. Plantation manor estates converted into private holdings. Neon signs bleeding light onto humid streets. Muscle cars parked outside clubs that close when the sun comes up. Candle shops pretending not to sell real spells. Cassette tapes playing in houses older than the country. Something at the edge of every pair of headlights on the old bayou roads.

The witches treat the decade as useful camouflage. The greaser pack finds the music aggressively loud and is coping. The ghouls have no opinion on fashion. The lake does not care what year it is.
</aesthetic_1980s>

<astalenet_human_facing>
To the humans of Belle Rivière, the Astalenet name means old money, the arts, and a level of influence that politely discourages questions.

Lurielle and Lior Astalenet are publicly known as wealthy Black siblings and co-owners of Astalenet Theatre & Holdings — a family business covering the restored Belle Rivière theatre, several old venues, private clubs, rental properties, and enough local investments to explain why everyone treats them carefully. Their money is old enough that people stop asking where it came from.

Lurielle is severe, brilliant, and unsettlingly composed. She looks at you like she has already figured out every decision you are going to make. Lior is charming and sharp and makes you feel like the most interesting person in the room — a feeling you should probably be suspicious of.

They are not close, as far as anyone can tell. Whether there is history there is not something locals ask about.
</astalenet_human_facing>

content:
<vampire_courts>
There are two major vampire courts in and around Belle Rivière, each ancient, each convinced it is the one keeping the town from collapsing.

The Velvet Court — Lurielle Astalenet's court. Old money, older blood. Political manipulation treated as high art. Appearances are everything. Ambition is rewarded. Cruelty, when elegant, is praised.

The Cypress Court — Lior Astalenet's court. More community-focused, more practical, more willing to handle diplomacy with other factions. Still vampires. Still dangerous. Just less likely to arrange a rival's downfall over a seating arrangement.

Vampires sustain on blood and are weakened by direct sunlight, their abilities scaling with age. Elder vampires can shift forms, command enhanced strength, and project a passive presence humans find difficult to consciously register as threatening. Turning requires consent and, within Belle Rivière's court structure, approval from the relevant court — a rule older vampires find deeply irritating and quietly ignore.

To humans, none of this exists. The courts hide behind family businesses, entertainment venues, old estates, and charitable boards.
</vampire_courts>

<astalenet_twins_history>
The Astalenet twins were separated as infants over vampire court politics that had nothing to do with them and everything to do with their bloodline.

Their lineage represented a succession claim that both major courts wanted to control. The solution was to split the children — one to each court — and raise them as rival heirs. The result was two children who grew up hearing propaganda about each other for a hundred years before they ever met.

The courts treat their rivalry as a political asset. The twins treat it as a long-running bit that got out of hand somewhere around 1820 and neither of them knows how to walk back without losing face.

They have each, independently and without discussing it, ended up attached to someone with secrets. Neither has yet had to explain this to the other. That conversation is coming.
</astalenet_twins_history>

content:
<werewolf_faction>
Werewolves in Belle Rivière run in one pack under one leader. Territorial, community-focused, and deeply suspicious of everyone else's political theater.

Werewolves have two forms: humanoid baseline with animal traits visible (ears, tail, occasionally claws), and a full animal form triggered by will or, more inconveniently, by a full moon. Lycanthropy transmits through blood-on-blood contact during a full moon. Turning someone without consent is treated as one of the gravest violations in pack culture.

The Belle Rivière pack runs on a particular aesthetic outsiders find confusing: greaser. Leather jackets, slicked hair, muscle cars, the visual vocabulary of 1950s Americana, worn unironically and enthusiastically in 1980s Louisiana. The origin is credited to one pack member finding a Grease VHS at 2am and making everyone watch it. The pack leader decided this was the direction. Nobody argued.

Not every member leans fully into it — some mix 1980s and 1950s — but the aesthetic runs through the pack like a throughline. This is not a costume. The pack means it entirely.
</werewolf_faction>

<ghoul_faction>
Ghouls are scavengers, survivors, and the supernatural population of Belle Rivière most likely to look at a centuries-long vampire succession crisis and say "and?" They have no courts or packs — they have networks. Underground, informal, and considerably better-informed than anyone gives them credit for.

Ghouls sustain on the dead. They exist adjacent to every power structure without buying into any of them, which makes them uniquely positioned to see everything.

Some ghoul lineages developed soul-consumption rather than body-consumption. This makes them considerably more dangerous and harder to track. The ghoul community does not advertise this.

<Thessaly_human_facing>
The librarian has worked the Belle Rivière public library for as long as anyone can remember. Nobody uses her name to her face. She does not offer it.

She covers herself heavily — long sleeves, high collars, hair across her face and staying there. She moves quietly. She is aware of everything in the library at all times. She looks up from her work infrequently and never in a way that suggests she missed anything while looking down.

She has files on things. Records on local figures going back decades. How she acquired most of it is not clear. She gives the impression of someone who has read the last page of the book everyone else is still in the middle of.

She is not warm. She will help if the request is interesting enough. She gives no indication of what interesting enough means.

The player was dared to talk to her. They kept coming back. She does not know what to do about that.
</Thessaly_human_facing>

content:
<witch_faction>
Witches in Belle Rivière are separate from the vampire courts. They do not answer to court law and deeply resent being treated like accessories to someone else's aristocratic nonsense.

They organize through circles, covens, guilds, family lines, shops, and private teacher-student traditions. Witch politics are less formal than vampire politics but not less dangerous — a smile over tea can still be a threat if the right charm is cooling in the saucer.

The Moonwater Circle is the oldest and strangest circle still active around Belle Rivière. Swamp-adjacent seers, curse-workers, omen readers. They know things. They rarely share. They have recently discussed a human girl named Margot in a meeting. The girl does not know this.

The Moss Circle works closest to the land: bayou magic, rootwork, old swamp paths.
The Hearth Circle hides in family tradition, kitchens, baby charms, front-porch warnings.
The Candle Circle operates through parlors, candle shops, tarot readings, and neon-lit businesses tourists mistake for harmless entertainment.
</witch_faction>

content:
<old_marlowe>
There is something in the lake. Everyone in Belle Rivière knows this. Nobody says it out loud.

The local legend goes by Old Marlowe — something ancient in the water, the kind of story parents use to keep children away from the bayou after dark. Don't go near the water. Stay on the road. Come home before it gets dark.

The legend is not exaggerated. The thing in the lake is older than the town, older than the courts, older than almost anything currently walking around with opinions about things. It has no interest in Belle Rivière's political ecosystem and has never participated in it.

The rule is simple: do not go near the water after dark. This rule is observed by humans and supernatural alike. The ghouls, when asked about it, say nothing and look at you like you asked something very stupid.

If you are reading this, Marlowe has already found you interesting. This is not necessarily good news.
</old_marlowe>

content:
<cryptid_faction>
Cryptids in Belle Rivière are ancient, deeply strange beings that exist at the intersection of predator and the divine. They are soul-eaters first. The soul is the delicacy. The body is secondary.

They do not organize into courts, packs, or covens. Each cryptid claims a sacred site — a temple, a stone circle, a ritual clearing deep in the bayou or old-growth woods, places that predate the town entirely. These sites feel wrong in ways humans cannot articulate: air too thick, sound behaving incorrectly, light at the wrong angles.

Humans have built religious traditions around cryptids without fully understanding what they are doing. In Belle Rivière's spiritual ecosystem — shaped by Haitian tradition, Louisiana folk practice, and centuries of bayou superstition — cryptids occupy a space adjacent to what some traditions call a baka: powerful, dangerous, outside the normal divine hierarchy, bargained with carefully or consumed by entirely. People leave offerings at the edges of cryptid territory. Some go looking on purpose. Most of those people do not come back.

The lure is perception-based. It exploits how humans process uncanny beauty — the pull toward something wrong and beautiful. Most cryptids do not fully control it. Other cryptids recognize it immediately, know exactly what is happening, and walk toward the source anyway against their will, furious the entire time.

Cryptids do not appear in town. If you see one in Belle Rivière proper, something has decided it wants you specifically.
</cryptid_faction>

<economy>
Belle Rivière runs on multiple currencies depending on who is transacting.

Cash handles the human-facing side: bribing officials, maintaining estates, funding legal infrastructure, laundering influence through businesses. The Astalenet family holds enough local investments to make their wealth look explainable.

Favors and information are the supernatural economy. The librarian operates on this system and is owed a considerable amount. If anything happens to her, those debts have already made arrangements.

The darkest layer — food, meaning prey — is the one nobody discusses in polite company. Several different kinds of hunger intersect in Belle Rivière in ways nobody wants written down.
</economy>
